prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

The cycle lane is most positively rated on Physical Comfort and Ease of Use. Compared to the adjacent cycle path, the cycle lane has stronger lane markings which increases the Ease of Use for cyclists. Additionally, it runs on the road level next to the motor traffic and is usually better asphalted than cycle paths. This allows a more fluent cycling and increases the Physical Comfort. Interestingly, the cycle lane is rated slightly more negatively on Mental Comfort than on Interaction. A well marked cycle lane is often considered as a proper cycling facility that draws drivers’ attention to possible cyclists. However, although it separates from the motor traffic and, therefore, leads to less possible interactions, cyclists might perceive it as mentally uncomfortable because of a small width and a lack of feeling safe. Generally spoken, the less the cycling facility is separated the worse it is rated on the clusters. Surprisingly, the bicycle boulevard is evaluated similar to the least separated advisory lane, but with a much better rating in Mental Comfort. This indicates that a too weak separation can no longer induce a feeling of safety or Mental Comfort, and below this threshold of separation, cyclists might prefer bicycle boulevards which draw attention to cyclists as road users, but in principle have no separation at all. More concrete, cyclists may prefer no separation over a too weak one. Bicycle boulevards are also evaluated more positively than residential roads, although in Germany, bicycle boulevards are usually open for motorized traffic and the traffic regulations are, hence, the same as for residential roads. The only difference are traffic signs that highlight cyclists as road users who must not be endangered by motor vehicles, and that cyclists are allowed to cycle side by side (Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection, 2020). On the one hand, this may lead to a stronger self-confidence of the cyclists towards other road users. On the other hand, cyclists may associate a bicycle boulevard with even lower traffic volume, lower traffic speed, and more cooperative and careful interactions with other road users which increases their perception of Interaction, Environment, and Mental Comfort compared to the residential road. The shared footpath is evaluated neither good nor bad on all the clusters. The Mental and Physical Comfort are even lower than at bicycle boulevards and shared spaces. Cyclists may feel uncomfortable here as they cycle on a way which is mainly for walking, and cycling is only tolerated. Cyclists are, thus, in the position of the stronger road user that must be considerate towards the weaker and slower pedestrians. Also, cyclists need to watch out for people leaving buildings or properties and suddenly stepping onto the footpath. All this might be perceived as stressful and as hindering the cycling flow. Apart from these differences between these intersection designs, we used the same parameters for all other design elements whenever possible. For example, design elements such as cycle lane widths, number of car lanes or overall street width were not varied between the three layouts. 3.4. Test procedure The study was conducted in October and November 2022 at Digital Cube Test Center (DCTC) at TU Berlin. After a brief introduction and explanation of the procedure, participants were asked to mount the bicycle for a test ride to re-acquaint themselves with the equipment they had already used in the previous study phase several months earlier. For each of the three intersection designs for this study phase, we created a virtual city with three successive junctions of the corresponding design. Participants had three trials consisting of a ride through one of the virtual cities. These were presented in random order to control for sequence effects. Participants’ task for every trial was to turn right, go straight, and then turn left. These directions were additionally indicated by an arrow that appeared on the screen when approaching the junction. We assumed that using this order would increase complexity for each turning maneuver, allowing participants to easily accustom themselves to each junction design within each trial. Each trial was followed by a focused guideline-based interview to identify strengths, weaknesses, and possible improvements for the junction design used in that trial (see Fig. 3 for a schematic overview of the test procedure). After each participant’s last interview, we asked them to compare all junctions and to briefly repeat the main strengths and weaknesses for each junction (see Interview Guideline, Fig. 4). Per participant, we recorded 61 minutes of interview on average, resulting in 17 hours of audio recording in total. 3.5. Data analysis All interviews were transcribed using standard transcription rules by Dresing and Pehl (2018). Based on these transcripts, we conducted a qualitative content analysis using MaxQDA (VERBI, 2016). As described, we had participants’ socio-demographical data collected. Furthermore, we had already assigned participants to three different cycling typologies in the previous study phase (see Friel et al., 2023, 144).

As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort

- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.
 4. Output Format Requirements (Return JSON ONLY, no extra text):

Preliminary theory: relationship between safety, comfort, and comprehensibility Based on the statements from the interviews, we were able to observe interdependencies between the three evaluation criteria safety, comfort, and comprehensibility (see Fig. 18). We are not yet able to formulate a comprehensive theory about the relationships, causes and effects of the three criteria. However, data analysis provides a first impression in terms of a preliminary theory of the relationship between safety, comfort, and comprehensibility and how they affect the overall evaluation of cycling infrastructure. As described above, we analyzed if and how each topic affects participants’ rating regarding the three criteria. The cycle lane is most positively rated on Physical Comfort and Ease of Use. Compared to the adjacent cycle path, the cycle lane has stronger lane markings which increases the Ease of Use for cyclists. Additionally, it runs on the road level next to the motor traffic and is usually better asphalted than cycle paths. This allows a more fluent cycling and increases the Physical Comfort. Interestingly, the cycle lane is rated slightly more negatively on Mental Comfort than on Interaction. A well marked cycle lane is often considered as a proper cycling facility that draws drivers’ attention to possible cyclists. However, although it separates from the motor traffic and, therefore, leads to less possible interactions, cyclists might perceive it as mentally uncomfortable because of a small width and a lack of feeling safe. Generally spoken, the less the cycling facility is separated the worse it is rated on the clusters. Surprisingly, the bicycle boulevard is evaluated similar to the least separated advisory lane, but with a much better rating in Mental Comfort. This indicates that a too weak separation can no longer induce a feeling of safety or Mental Comfort, and below this threshold of separation, cyclists might prefer bicycle boulevards which draw attention to cyclists as road users, but in principle have no separation at all. More concrete, cyclists may prefer no separation over a too weak one. Bicycle boulevards are also evaluated more positively than residential roads, although in Germany, bicycle boulevards are usually open for motorized traffic and the traffic regulations are, hence, the same as for residential roads. The only difference are traffic signs that highlight cyclists as road users who must not be endangered by motor vehicles, and that cyclists are allowed to cycle side by side (Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection, 2020). On the one hand, this may lead to a stronger self-confidence of the cyclists towards other road users. On the other hand, cyclists may associate a bicycle boulevard with even lower traffic volume, lower traffic speed, and more cooperative and careful interactions with other road users which increases their perception of Interaction, Environment, and Mental Comfort compared to the residential road. The shared footpath is evaluated neither good nor bad on all the clusters. The Mental and Physical Comfort are even lower than at bicycle boulevards and shared spaces. Cyclists may feel uncomfortable here as they cycle on a way which is mainly for walking, and cycling is only tolerated. Cyclists are, thus, in the position of the stronger road user that must be considerate towards the weaker and slower pedestrians. Also, cyclists need to watch out for people leaving buildings or properties and suddenly stepping onto the footpath. All this might be perceived as stressful and as hindering the cycling flow. Test procedure The study was conducted in October and November 2022 at Digital Cube Test Center (DCTC) at TU Berlin. After a brief introduction and explanation of the procedure, participants were asked to mount the bicycle for a test ride to re-acquaint themselves with the equipment they had already used in the previous study phase several months earlier. For each of the three intersection designs for this study phase, we created a virtual city with three successive junctions of the corresponding design. Participants had three trials consisting of a ride through one of the virtual cities. These were presented in random order to control for sequence effects. Participants’ task for every trial was to turn right, go straight, and then turn left. These directions were additionally indicated by an arrow that appeared on the screen when approaching the junction. We assumed that using this order would increase complexity for each turning maneuver, allowing participants to easily accustom themselves to each junction design within each trial. Each trial was followed by a focused guideline-based interview to identify strengths, weaknesses, and possible improvements for the junction design used in that trial (see Fig. 3 for a schematic overview of the test procedure). After each participant’s last interview, we asked them to compare all junctions and to briefly repeat the main strengths and weaknesses for each junction (see Interview Guideline, Fig. 4). Per participant, we recorded 61 minutes of interview on average, resulting in 17 hours of audio recording in total. 3.5. Data analysis All interviews were transcribed using standard transcription rules by Dresing and Pehl (2018). Based on these transcripts, we conducted a qualitative content analysis using MaxQDA (VERBI, 2016). As described, we had participants’ socio-demographical data collected. Furthermore, we had already assigned participants to three different cycling typologies in the previous study phase (see Friel et al., 2023, 144).
